lead: A walk is an ordered list of vertices and edges where each edge joins the vertices on either side of it. Adding restrictions gives trails, paths, circuits and cycles. Connectivity asks whether one vertex can reach another by following edges. These ideas matter in road routing, UPI transaction networks, chip wiring and power-grid reliability, where a single weak link can split a network into separate pieces.
prereq: You need: graph vocabulary such as vertices, edges, degree and subgraph from 6.1.

blocks.text: A walk in a graph is a sequence v0, e1, v1, …, ek, vk, where each edge ei joins vi−1 to vi. The length of the walk is k, the number of edges used. A walk is closed when v0 = vk; otherwise it is open. Vertices and edges may repeat in a walk.

Add restrictions. A trail repeats no edge. A path repeats no vertex. A circuit is a closed trail. A cycle is a closed walk with no repeated vertex except the start equals the end. In a simple graph a cycle has length at least 3. Some syllabi call a circuit a closed trail; a few use circuit for any closed walk, so check the definition in your notes.

items: Every path is a trail, because no repeated vertex forces no repeated edge.
Every cycle is a circuit, but a circuit can repeat vertices, so it need not be a cycle.

blocks.text: A graph is connected when a path exists between every pair of vertices. A component is a maximal connected subgraph. A disconnected graph has two or more components. The graph in the figure is connected and has one component.

items: Remove vertex v to form G − v. If G − v has more components than G, then v is a cut vertex (articulation point).
Remove edge e to form G − e. If G − e has more components than G, then e is a bridge.
Repeat for each vertex and each edge to find all cuts.

blocks.text: Vertex connectivity κ(G) is the minimum number of vertices whose removal disconnects G or leaves one vertex. Edge connectivity λ(G) is the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects G. For a connected graph with at least two vertices, κ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ δ(G).

blocks.where: κ(G) is vertex connectivity; λ(G) is edge connectivity; δ(G) is the minimum degree of G.

blocks.text: In the figure δ(G) = 1, κ(G) = 1 and λ(G) = 1. A bridge gives λ(G) = 1. The inequality is a quick check, not a full computation.

sections.h3: Directed graphs: reachability and strong connectivity

blocks.text: In a directed graph, a directed walk follows edge directions. A directed path repeats no vertex. Vertex v is reachable from u when a directed path runs from u to v. Reachability is not symmetric: one-way roads and one-way UPI settlement links are examples.

A directed graph is strongly connected when every ordered pair (u, v) has a directed path from u to v. It is weakly connected when replacing every directed edge by an undirected edge gives a connected graph. Strong connectivity implies weak connectivity; weak connectivity does not imply strong connectivity.

items: Strong component: a maximal strongly connected subgraph.
Directed cycle: a closed directed walk with no repeated vertex except the start.
u → v and v → u is strong on two vertices; u → v alone is weak, not strong.

figure.caption: Edges A–B and B–C are bridges, and B and C are cut vertices. The triangle C–D–E gives a cycle; A–B–C–E is a path of length 3.

spec.aria: A connected graph on five vertices A to E with bridges A B and B C, cut vertices B and C, and a triangle C D E.

examples.question: In the graph with vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges AB, BC, CD, DE, CE, find a path from A to E, one cycle, the cut vertices and the bridges.
steps: List the vertices V = {A, B, C, D, E} and edges AB, BC, CD, DE, CE.
Path A–B–C–E uses edges AB, BC, CE. The vertex list is A, B, C, E: all distinct. Length = 3 edges.
Cycle C–D–E–C uses edges CD, DE, EC. Start and end are C; D and E appear once. Length = 3 edges.
Cut vertex test for B: G − B has components {A} and {C, D, E}, so 2 components against 1 in G. B is a cut vertex.
Cut vertex test for C: G − C has components {A, B} and {D, E}, so 2 components. C is a cut vertex.
Removing A, D or E leaves one component, so they are not cut vertices.
Bridge test for AB: G − AB has components {A} and {B, C, D, E}, so 2 components. AB is a bridge.
Bridge test for BC: G − BC has components {A, B} and {C, D, E}, so 2 components. BC is a bridge.
Removing CD, DE or CE leaves the graph connected, so those edges are not bridges.
examples.answer: A path A–B–C–E has length 3; a cycle C–D–E–C has length 3; there are 2 cut vertices (B, C) and 2 bridges (AB, BC).

traps: A closed walk with a repeated vertex is not a cycle. The cycle rule allows only v<sub>0</sub> = v<sub>k</sub>; every other vertex appears once.
A bridge is an edge; a cut vertex is a vertex. Removing either increases the number of components.
A trail may repeat vertices. A path may not. A walk may repeat both.
Weak connectivity of a directed graph does not give reachability in both directions. Check ordered pairs for strong connectivity.
The inequality κ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ δ(G) assumes a connected graph with at least two vertices; complete graphs and single vertices use special conventions.

quiz.q: Define the length of a walk. What is the length of the walk A, AB, B, BC, C, CE, E?
quiz.a: Length is the number of edges used. The walk uses AB, BC and CE, so its length is 3.

quiz.q: Why is every path a trail, but a trail need not be a path?
quiz.a: A path has no repeated vertex, so it cannot repeat an edge. A trail may repeat vertices, for example A–B–C–B, so it need not be a path.

quiz.q: In a graph with edges AB, BC, CD, DA, AC, find one cycle and a path from B to D that does not use C.
quiz.a: One cycle is A–C–D–A using AC, CD, DA. A path from B to D avoiding C is B–A–D using BA and AD, length 2.

quiz.q: A connected graph has a bridge e. Can it be 2-edge-connected? Explain using λ(G).
quiz.a: No. Removing e increases the number of components, so the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects the graph is 1. Thus λ(G) = 1, not at least 2.

quiz.q: Directed graph edges: u → v, v → w, w → u and x → u. Is it strongly connected? Is it weakly connected?
quiz.a: Vertices u, v, w reach each other, but x reaches u and no directed path returns to x. So the graph is not strongly connected. Ignoring directions gives a connected graph, so it is weakly connected.

quiz.q: State the relation between κ(G), λ(G) and δ(G).
quiz.a: For a connected graph with at least two vertices, κ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ δ(G).

quiz.q: In the chapter figure, remove vertex C. List the components and decide whether C is a cut vertex.
quiz.a: G − C has components {A, B} and {D, E}. The graph had one component, so removal gives two components. C is a cut vertex.

quiz.q: What is a component of a graph?
quiz.a: A component is a maximal connected subgraph. Every vertex lies in exactly one component.

beyond: Not for the exam. Strong components power cycle detection in package managers and build systems: a dependency cycle is a directed cycle. Bridges and cut vertices identify weak links in power grids, road networks and sensor networks, and bridge-finding runs in linear time. Search next for Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, strongly connected components, and the condensation of a directed graph.
